title: SEX, SCANDAL, CONCUBINES, PROSTITUTES, ADULTERY, AND GRACE: Why Did God Leave All of This in the Bible?
paragraphs:
SEX, SCANDAL, CONCUBINES, PROSTITUTES, ADULTERY, AND GRACE: Why Did God Leave All of This in the Bible?
The Bible could have hidden the bedroom scandals, broken families, sexual failures, exploited women, prostitutes, adulterers, and ruined reputations. It didn’t. And the reason may completely change the way you understand grace.
There are pages in the Bible we almost wish were easier to explain.
Pages we would probably remove if we were responsible for God's public relations.
Jacob has Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah.
Judah sleeps with a woman he believes is a prostitute—only to discover that she is Tamar, his daughter-in-law.
Rahab is introduced as a prostitute.
Samson repeatedly walks toward women and desires that help pull him toward destruction.
David takes Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and then arranges Uriah's death after she becomes pregnant.
Solomon accumulates wives and concubines on a staggering scale.
The prophets sometimes describe Israel's spiritual unfaithfulness using shocking sexual imagery.
when Matthew opens the New Testament and begins announcing Jesus Christ to the world, he does something that should stop us in our tracks.
He brings some of the scandal back.
And then, instead of simply saying Bathsheba, Matthew writes:
The wound is not airbrushed out of the family history.

Why would a holy God allow Scripture to preserve stories containing prostitution, concubinage, adultery, sexual exploitation, lust, betrayal, incestuous situations, shattered marriages, abused power, and generations of family dysfunction?
Why not give us heroes without stains?
Why not give us saints without embarrassing histories?
Perhaps because if God had given us a Bible filled only with polished people, some of us would eventually conclude that there was no place in it for people like us.
And that is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because this article isn't really about their scandal.
Eventually, the Bible turns the mirror around.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody knows what happened behind the closed door.
Nobody knows what you did after midnight.
Nobody knows what happened before you became a Christian.
Nobody knows what you are still fighting after becoming one.
Maybe your sin wasn't sexual at all.
Maybe people at church know the version of you that knows when to smile, when to raise a hand during worship, when to say “God is good,” and when to post a Bible verse.
But God knows the unedited version.
He still invited you to come.
That does not mean God calls darkness light.
It means grace is greater than the darkness it exposes.
The Bible records many things that God never approves.

Scripture telling us that patriarchs had concubines does not mean concubinage represents God's creation design. Jesus Himself reaches behind humanity's broken arrangements and points back toward God's intention “from the beginning” when discussing marriage (Matthew 19:4–6; compare Genesis 2:24).
Scripture showing David's actions toward Bathsheba does not celebrate David.
The biblical narrator gives us God's verdict with devastating simplicity:
“But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.”
David may be king, but the King above David is not impressed by his title.
David's hidden evil is dragged into the light.
Yet David eventually says something extraordinarily important:
“The LORD also has put away your sin.”
That is the frightening and beautiful tension of biblical grace.
God does not pretend David's evil never happened.
And yet God is also capable of forgiving the repentant sinner.
Grace is not God shrugging at sin.
That distinction becomes even clearer at the cross.
The Greek New Testament uses a magnificent word:
“The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”
Jesus does not need to lie about what you did in order to love you.
He doesn't have to rename adultery.
He doesn't have to rename lust.
He doesn't have to rename exploitation.
He doesn't have to rename fornication, greed, drunkenness, hatred, deception, idolatry, or pride.
He can call sin what it is...
and still call sinners to Himself.
That is what makes the Gospel so staggering.
We often think our greatest hope is that nobody ever discovers the truth about us.
The Gospel offers something infinitely greater:
God already knows the truth about us.
Read the genealogy in Matthew 1 carefully.
We tend to rush through genealogies because they look like lists of names.
Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar.
David fathered Solomon “by the wife of Uriah.”
Do not misunderstand what Matthew is doing.

The genealogy does not mean everyone's actions in those stories were sinful, nor does it reduce these women to sexual scandal. Ruth, for example, is presented in Scripture as a woman of remarkable loyalty and character. Neither should every person involved in another person's wrongdoing be treated as equally culpable.
The human history into which Christ entered was not sanitized.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because sin matters so much that humanity needs a Savior.
This is one of the reasons the Bible's brutal honesty matters.
Human propaganda normally protects its heroes.
Paul openly tells us that he persecuted the church.
The Bible refuses to construct a museum of flawless human beings.
Because there is only one spotless Hero at the center of this story.
That is why the Hebrew language of the Old Testament gives us another beautiful word worth remembering:
It is a rich covenant word often translated with ideas such as steadfast love, lovingkindness, faithfulness, or covenant loyalty depending on context.
David cries in Psalm 51 after Nathan confronts him:
“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love.”
“God, explain why my behavior wasn't actually that bad.”
He doesn't point toward everything good he previously accomplished.
It is not being sorry that screenshots survived.
It is not regretting that your spouse found out.
It is not sadness because your reputation collapsed.
Biblical repentance turns toward God with the truth.
No more hiding behind religious vocabulary.
And here is where someone reading this may need to stop.
Because you have spent years trying to bury something Jesus wants you to surrender.
“If they knew what I used to be...”
“If they knew what I still struggle with...”
But the most important sentence is not:
And the God who knows calls sinners to repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
There is a difference between hiding sin and having sin forgiven.
Hiding says, “Maybe darkness can protect me.”
The Gospel says, “Come into the light.”
God “is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
The Greek verb behind “confess,” ὁμολογέω — homologeō, carries the idea of acknowledging or confessing.
We come before God agreeing with the truth about our sin.
Not because tears pay the debt.
Not because we punish ourselves long enough to convince God we are serious.
The Gospel is not the announcement that damaged people can repair themselves if they try harder.
The Gospel announces that the Son of God entered our ruined world, lived without sin, died for sinners, and rose again.
At the cross, grace stops being sentimental.
Look closely at Calvary and you will never again be able to say God doesn't take sin seriously.
Look closely at Calvary and you will never again be able to say God cannot love sinners.
The cross tells the truth about how terrible sin is...
and how far God was willing to go to redeem sinners.
Maybe that is why Scripture leaves the scandals in.
Not so we can gossip about dead sinners.
Not so we can use biblical failure as permission for our own.
Not so we can turn broken women into sermon props or powerful men into untouchable heroes.
God's Word forces us to confront the catastrophic seriousness of sin while showing us the astonishing reach of redemption.
Joshua 2 identifies her as a prostitute.
The New Testament does not erase her past.
Hebrews 11 remembers Rahab—but now the emphasis is her faith.
James 2 remembers her actions flowing from that faith.
Matthew places her in the genealogy leading to Christ.
But her past does not get the final word.
Some people will always introduce you by your worst chapter.
Jesus is capable of writing another one.
This does not mean earthly consequences disappear.
Forgiveness does not magically restore every broken relationship.
Repentance may require confession, restitution, accountability, boundaries, counseling, pastoral help, or accepting consequences.
Grace is not an escape hatch from responsibility.
Grace transforms what we do with responsibility.
The forgiven person no longer needs to protect the lie at all costs.
They can begin walking in the light.
Because identity no longer has to be built around maintaining the illusion of innocence.
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.”
Paul did not erase his history.
He turned his history into a testimony about mercy.
You are more sinful than self-righteousness wants to admit.
And Christ is more merciful than shame wants you to believe.
That is why grace is so offensive to religious pride.
We want grace for ourselves and justice for everybody whose sins disgust us.
Then Jesus tells stories about prodigals coming home.
The younger son in Luke 15 burns through his inheritance in reckless living.
“I have sinned against heaven and before you.”
He comes home expecting perhaps to become a servant.
But while he is still far away...
And the father calls for the robe.
Because the lost son came home.
“This my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”
Maybe you have been living among the pigs while still remembering Father's house.
Maybe pornography has been eating your soul quietly.
Maybe adultery has fractured everything you once promised to protect.
Maybe you have been sleeping with someone you know you should surrender to God.
Maybe sexual abuse was committed against you, and religious people made you carry shame that belonged to the person who harmed you.
Being sinned against is not the same thing as committing that sin.
What someone did to you is not a stain that makes you undesirable to Christ.
Maybe none of those are your story.
Maybe your scandal is hidden behind respectability.
Maybe you have never committed adultery physically, but Jesus' words about lust in Matthew 5 make you deeply uncomfortable.
Maybe your body remained in church while your imagination lived somewhere else.
Maybe your sin is the self-righteousness that looks at prostitutes, adulterers, addicts, sexually broken people, and ruined marriages and quietly says:
There is room at the cross for the sexually broken.
There is room for the sexually betrayed.
There is room for the person carrying memories they wish they could erase.
There is room for the hypocrite who finally stops pretending.
There is room for the prodigal.
There is room for the religious older brother.
But there is no room for pretending we do not need Jesus.
That may be the secret buried underneath all those uncomfortable biblical stories.
God did not preserve scandal so we could become entertained by sin.
And truth reveals why we desperately need grace.
If Scripture had hidden David's adultery and abuse of power, we might have admired a manufactured David.
Instead, Scripture lets David collapse before us.
Then Scripture points beyond David toward the Son of David who never collapses.
Solomon multiplied wives despite the covenant warnings given to Israel's kings.
Christ keeps standing at the center of redemption.
And perhaps the greatest scandal in the Bible is not that sinners sinned.
We already know sinners do that.
The astonishing scandal of grace is that the Holy One chose to save them.
Not by pretending evil is good.
The innocent One suffering for the guilty.
The rejected One opening the way for prodigals to return home.
The crucified Christ rising from the grave.
And now the invitation reaches us.
You do not need a cleaner history before coming to Jesus.
You do not need to rewrite yesterday before coming.
You need the One who can redeem what yesterday became.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same heartbeat:
Not by pretending the scandal never existed.
Not necessarily by erasing every earthly consequence.
Jesus rewrites everything because sin no longer has to possess the final sentence.
What chapter are you still trying to hide from God?
What secret keeps whispering that you can never really come home?
What sin have you been managing instead of confessing?
What wound have you mistaken for your identity?
What would happen if tonight you stopped performing...
“Jesus Christ, have mercy on me. I have sinned. I cannot save myself. Forgive me, cleanse me, change me, and teach me to follow You.”

And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't have to publish the details of your private sin. Wisdom matters. Some things belong in confidential conversations with trustworthy pastoral, professional, or appropriate support.
But you can still take one small step out of hiding.
And when you see somebody else saying “pray for me,” don't interrogate them.
There is already enough gossip in the world.
Let the people of Jesus become known for carrying one another toward Christ.
Come back and remember: conviction says, “Bring it to Jesus.” Condemnation tells you there is no point coming back.
You may never know who reads it at 2:13 in the morning.
You may never know whose finger stops scrolling.
You may never know whose secret almost destroyed them.
You may never know who finally whispers:
We want this community to remain a place of daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Christ alone is our Savior, and Christians glorify God in countless acts of faith, obedience, generosity, service, worship, and love.
Carry hope into somebody else's darkness.
Tell the ashamed there is a cross.
Tell prodigals the Father still calls them home.
Tell the self-righteous that they need mercy too.
Tell the wounded that what was done to them does not have to become their identity.
Tell the repentant that Christ receives sinners.
Tell the world that the Bible didn't hide the scandal...
because God wanted broken people to know that scandal does not have to be the end of their story.
And if you belong to Jesus...
The page you are most ashamed of may become the very place where someone finally sees how powerful the grace of Jesus Christ really is.
